newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: YEAREND-Asian firms seek more debt as funding needs grow.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Asian firms seek more debt as funding needs grow.

text.p: Infrastructure companies from Asian economies are increasingly relying on credit to fund mega-projects, but the absence of active secondary markets restricts the choice of debt products they can use, analysts and bankers said.

Realising an opportunity to attract investors, Asian nations are vying with each other to remove stumbling blocks to the development of their respective financial sectors, but progress is slow, particularly for the debt market, they said.
Bankers estimate that Southeast Asia and South Asia alone will need several hundred billion dollars over the next few years to build their infrastructure.

For the moment, banks face issuers' reluctance, legal hurdles, high taxes, rigid interest rate structures and greater credit risk in the region's economies even as their infrastructure funding requirement grows sharply.

But these problems are not stopping either international banks or domestic financial institutions from lending to infrastructure projects, many of which are privatised but backed by the government, analysts said.

"Most of the debt issued here is simple credit. It does not matter what you call the product, bonds or FRNs (floating rate notes), it is still basic debt (like loans)," said Lee Soon Kie, managing director of investment bank Schroders in Thailand.
Bankers involved in infrastructure projects in the region said the same story extended to most countries in Asia.
Most bonds and FRNs issued in the past have not been traded at all, they said.
MALAYSIA TO THE FORE
One of the biggest infrastructure projects of the region is Malaysia's 15 billion ringgit ($6.0 billion) Bakun hydroelectric project in Sarawak.
Though yet to announce financing details, the project is expected to be funded in the debt-to-equity ratio of 60:40.
Analysts say Bakun will do a large private debt securities (PDS), or bonds, issue as part of its financing.
Ekran, the project's promoter, announced last week that it was planning to list Bakun Hydroelectric Corporation Bhd with an issue of 1.5 billion shares at two ringgit or more each.
Malaysia, home to some of the biggest infrastructure projects in the region, is extensively using debt to fund them.

Its mega-projects include an $8.0 billion new federal capital, a $3.6 billion airport and the $1.2 billion Kuala Lumpur City Centre featuring the world's tallest buildings, the 450-metre tall Petronas twin towers.
Analysts said the financing of all these projects is structured in the debt-to-equity ratio of 2:1 to 4:1.

The twin towers have gone in for at least $660 million in loans, part of which is to be replaced with a large PDS issue. The Kuala Lumpur International Airport Bhd has already raised $880 million from issue of 20-year Islamic bonds and part of the funding for the federal capital is expected to come from issue of government bonds.
OTHER COUNTRIES FEATURE TOO
In Bangkok, a mass rapid transit system's $1.68 billion cost is being partly financed through $1.02 billion in loans and $100 million in subordinated debt issued by its private promoter Tanayong Plc.

Tanayong's financing arrangements for Bangkok Mass Transit System Corporation Ltd (BTSC) are complicated by its concession contract which states that it must keep a majority of BTSC's shares up to the project's completion.

It has raised $200 million through a private share placement, and a zero-coupon bond issue for $110 million to Tanayong's shareholders which are convertible to BTSC shares upon the project's completion.
Another 18 percent of BTSC's equity or 136 million shares will be offered to public in 1997 to raise $200 million.

Taiwan's Second North Highway, costing T$176.7 billion ($6.43 billion) and one of the island's largest infrastructure projects, has issued T$50 billion ($1.82 billion), or 28.3 percent of the total cost, in government bonds.

"The government has issued T$50 billion in government bonds to help finance the project, and we can self-pay the other cost by collecting tolls from our First highway," said Yeh Yung-cheng, accounting department chief of the national expressway engineering bureau in the Ministry of Transportation and Communication.
The First Highway collects between T$20 and T$30 billion (US$0.73-1.09 billion) in tolls a year, Yeh said.

In Manila, Citra Metro Manila Tollways Corp, a joint venture between the Philippine National Construction Corp and PT Citra group of Indonesia, is raising $192 million in loans to partly finance its $513 million tollway project. The remainder will come from equity (20 percent) and quasi-equity in the form of convertible bonds (30 percent).
India's largest privatised project, a 2,450 MW power plant will be built by Enron Corporation of the U.S. at a cost of $2.5 billion, funded almost entirely from offshore sources.
"A large number of infrastructure debt is straight loans, government bonds or equity-linked bonds," a regional banker based in Singapore said.
SECONDARY MARKET CONCERNS ADDRESSED
Most countries in the region are also setting up infrastructure, both legal and physical, to promote active secondary market in debt instruments.
The Malaysia Monetary Exchange to trade in interest rate futures has been launched. It is soon expected to start trading government bond futures.
Malaysia will also launch benchmark bonds of varying tenures in early 1997 which will help in pricing corporate issues and improve liquidity in the secondary market.
Thailand too is setting up a futures market and has launched a bond dealers club to promote trading in debt.
In the Philippines, the private sector is lobbying to get rid of a 20 percent witholding tax, which is preventing the growth of a secondary market.
The Bankers Association of the Philippines is trying to tackle the liquidity problem by setting up an automated system for trading in government securities.
Low credit rating for Philippine debt has also been a problem but it's improving and expectations are that rating agencies will announce an upgrade soon, analysts said.

In July, Taiwan's watchdog Securities and Exchange Commission helped the bond market establish a nationwide yield-to-maturity matching system, which is now used by 26 major bond trading securities brokerages.

An exception to the trend, Taiwan's bond market turnover started to exceed the stock market in 1992. In 1995, the bond market turnover was T$20.8 trillion (US$756 billion), more than double the stock market's T$10.15 trillion (US$369 billion), according to the central bank statistics.
